<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
I've read it. Here's my summary, to check I have the same thing:

**What it argues:** Varga and Holm re-analyse the Halden microdata and report four problems.

1. **Attrition.** 7 of the 9 withdrawals came *after* the schedule began, mostly citing workload. The working paper said they withdrew in preparation for scheduling reasons.
2. **Output measure.** In the 23 organisations that submitted records, manager-reported output was 3.8 points higher than the records showed. This was true in 19 of the 23.
3. **Hours.** Time tracking in 27 organisations shows actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%. In the 17 organisations with both records and tracking, the per-hour gain falls from 23.4% to 10.8%.
4. **Revenue.** Deflated by 4.1% CPI, revenue fell about 2.6% in real terms.

They also argue the "sector-general" claim is an artifact of dividing by hours, citing Varden's counter result. They attribute the remaining ~11% to novelty, based on the energy decline. They dismiss Varden's meetings analysis as a post hoc subgroup finding. They conclude that per-hour gains from reduced-hours schemes are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty."

**Arithmetic.** I checked the figures and they hold:
- Table 2: 98.7/0.8 = +23.4%, 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 34.6/40.3 = 0.859, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%, 34.8/40.4 = 0.861, and 95.4/86.1 = +10.8%.
- Revenue: 1.014/1.041 gives −2.6%.

There is one exception, in point 3 below.

**My overall view.** Sections 1–5 are good work. They went back to the primary data, documented each correction, and stated the limits of each subset. Sections 6–8 make the opposite mistake to the one they correct in Halden. Halden overstated a provisional result. This comment closes an open question as negative, dismisses a live hypothesis, and draws a conclusion its own numbers don't reach.

## What it establishes, at full weight

- **Halden misreported its attrition.** This is the comment's most important contribution. A working paper describing post-start, output-related withdrawals as "preparation phase, chiefly scheduling" is a factual error, not a matter of interpretation. Halden should correct it.
- **Manager ratings run high.** The record-based comparison shows an upward bias of about 4 points, consistent in direction. This confirms what Halden's own limitation 3 hinted at.
- **The scheduled-hours denominator inflated the gain.** Measured actual hours confirm this. The roughly 12.6-point gap between 23.4% and 10.8% matches Varden's directly measured gap of 22% versus 12.5% on the same basis.
- **The revenue figure was misleading.** One caveat: CPI is a rough deflator for organisations whose revenue comes from services and, for non-profits, grants. A sector-specific price index would be better, though probably not much different.
- **The sector critique holds.** It is now supported by two independent sources: Halden's records subset (retail −11.2%, though only n = 3) and Varden's randomised counter stratum.

## Where it overreaches

**1. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the comment's own numbers.** After every correction they could make, the estimate is **+10.8%**, not zero. The data note correctly says the subsets aren't representative, which cuts both ways: the true figure could be higher or lower. Adding "in our assessment" doesn't change the claim. Their evidence supports "much smaller than reported and of uncertain durability." It does not support "entirely an artifact."

**2. It leaves out the strongest evidence against its conclusion.** The comment calls Varden's counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature." But Varden's case-processing stratum comes from the same randomised trial, uses the same administrative records and timesheets, and has a tighter interval: **+12.5% per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4)**. That design rules out both selection and measurement as explanations, which are two of the three artifacts the comment names. Only novelty remains, and Varden measured at month nine. By the comment's own extrapolation, energy would have been near baseline by then, yet the gain was still present. Citing one stratum of a trial as definitive while omitting the other is the same selective reading the comment criticises in Halden.

**3. The hours breakdown doesn't add up.** The two sources given are +0.7 hours per day over four days (2.8 hours) and 1.6 hours logged on the day off. Added to 32 scheduled hours, that gives about **36.4 hours**, not the reported 34.6. Starting from the 40.3-hour baseline instead gives about 36.6. Either a component or the total is wrong, and the direction matters. If actual hours were nearer 36.5, the fall is about 9.5%, and the per-hour gain shrinks further, to about +5% on record-based output. This needs checking against the microdata before Table 2 can be relied on.

**4. The abstract says attrition was corrected, but it wasn't.** The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%, and the first three include attrition. Table 2 corrects only output and hours, and attrition is never quantified. A simple bound shows how much it could matter, counting by organisation and taking the 10.8% at face value:

| Assumed per-hour change in the 9 withdrawals | Overall estimate across all 70 |
|---|---|
| 0% | about 9.4% |
| −10% | about 8.1% |
| −73% | 0% |

The withdrawn organisations would need to have lost almost three-quarters of their per-hour output to erase the gain. Attrition biases the estimate upward, but it cannot plausibly account for the whole gain. A properly weighted bound by employee count would be worth reporting.

**5. The novelty argument skips the direct test.** The case rests on drawing a straight line through two survey points on energy, a self-reported measure that is not output. (That line actually reaches zero at about month 9, not 10.) But Halden collected the output index **monthly**, and the authors have the microdata. Whether output per hour declined from month to month is the direct test of novelty, and they didn't run it. Saying "the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" moves the burden rather than weighing the evidence. Honestly stated, durability is **open**. It would be settled by the monthly output trajectory, Varden's 24-month follow-up, and actual hours tracked over time.

**6. Section 7 misdescribes the Varden analysis.**
- **Not post hoc.** The meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed. They weren't "selected for analysis after the results were known."
- **Not a subgroup.** The seven offices are the whole treated case-processing arm, not a chosen subset.
- **Not claimed as a mechanism.** Varden explicitly said it cannot establish a mechanism and registered a confirmatory test.

The comment also omits that Halden's interviews independently point the same way: 47 of 58 managers cited cutting meetings. Each source is weak. Together they make a live hypothesis with a registered test pending. Saying "it should not be cited as a mechanism" is right. Saying it should be dropped as an explanation is premature.

**7. A smaller point on the output records.** Some records are "billable hours delivered." In a trial about hours, that measure partly tracks the input. Professional-services organisations could show smaller per-hour gains on records for this reason alone. It would be worth separating results by record type.

## Updating my earlier reads

- My Halden review assumed the withdrawals happened during preparation, as the paper stated. I should have treated that as a claim to check, and the microdata show it was wrong.
- My estimate of "probably inflated by around 10 points" was close (12.6). I guessed a real decline in revenue, and the comment confirms one, with the deflator caveat above.
- My earlier calculated interval of r = 0.71 across seven offices (roughly −0.1 to 0.95) still stands. The meetings evidence is weak, but that is a reason to test it, not to dismiss it.

## The combined picture across all three papers

- **Settled:**
  - Halden's headline was substantially overstated.
  - Dividing by scheduled hours inflates per-hour gains by roughly 10 points.
  - Manager ratings run high.
  - In presence-bound work, cutting hours without extra staff reduces output and service.
- **Supported but not settled:** a gain per actual hour of roughly 10–12% in work not tied to presence. Two independent sources converge on this: Halden's corrected subset and Varden's randomised case-processing stratum. The Halden half is weakened by the hours inconsistency in point 3.
- **Open:**
  - Durability (novelty versus a lasting effect).
  - Mechanism (rest versus removing low-value time).
  - Generalisation beyond volunteers and one county.

I can draft a short reply to the comment covering points 2–6, or a one-page synthesis of the three papers, if either would help.
